AtModel.description:
Where an `insert` writes: a point, or a piece of text to hang off.

The point is the BASELINE ORIGIN of the first line written -- where the bottom left
of the first glyph sits, not the top left of a text box. That is how every
coordinate in this engine is expressed (a span's `origin`, `/v1/text`'s span
geometry), so the x/y of a span read out of a document can be used here unchanged;
and it is the one of the two that does not move when `fit` shrinks the size.

after.description: Anchor text to insert after; the first occurrence on the page wins, and the style is inherited from it.
after.title: After

placement.description: With `after`: 'inline' writes one space past the anchor's right edge on its own baseline; 'below' writes at the anchor line's left edge, one leading down.
placement.title: Placement

x.description: Baseline origin x. Points from the page's left edge, or a fraction of the page width when units='fraction'.
x.title: X

y.description: Baseline origin y: where the first line sits, measured from the page's TOP edge (PDF viewer convention, as every bbox and span origin in this API). A fraction of the page height when units='fraction'.
y.title: Y

AtModel.title: AtModel

get.description:
Audit metadata for the account's jobs, newest first, no file contents.

Paged by ``cursor``: the ``job_id`` of the last row returned. Job ids are
ULIDs, so ``id < cursor`` is both the pagination predicate and a
chronological one -- no offset, and a page is stable while new jobs
arrive.

``since`` is applied in Python rather than in SQL on purpose: SQLite
stores ``DateTime(timezone=True)`` naive (see ``db.as_utc``), so an
offset-aware bound in a WHERE clause compares wrongly. Because the rows
come back newest-first, the first row older than ``since`` ends the page
and nothing qualifying can be below it.

parameters.description: the job_id of the last row of the previous page
